articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. This action targets entities involved in the theft and misappropriation of American intellectual property, a critical component of U.S. economic and national security.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses aim to provide clarity and minimize unintended consequences for legitimate transactions, allowing certain activities that would otherwise be prohibited under the new sanctions.

The PAIPA legislation underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft, which poses a significant threat to American innovation and competitiveness on a global scale.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This update aims to clarify existing sanctions policies and provide guidance for specific transactions involving Venezuela.

The amendment to the General License and the accompanying FAQ are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to fine-tune its sanctions programs, responding to evolving circumstances and ensuring that humanitarian aid and other permissible activities can continue.
These adjustments reflect a dynamic approach to Venezuela sanctions, balancing pressure on the regime with considerations for the Venezuelan populace and certain economic engagements.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting illicit activities or undermining U.S. foreign policy objectives in these regions.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These accompanying documents provide crucial guidance on the scope of the new sanctions and outline permissible activities, aiming to mitigate unintended impacts on legitimate trade and humanitarian efforts.

The new sanctions packages on Iran and Cuba signal a continued focus by the U.S. Treasury on these jurisdictions, with potential implications for energy and commodity exports, as well as shipping, insurance, and financial channels.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-related Designation, Signaling Potential Shift in Policy
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a potential shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela, following the lifting of sanctions on Jorge Rodriguez, president of Venezuela's National Assembly.

The delisting of Jorge Rodriguez, brother of acting President Delcy Rodriguez, comes amid reports of warming relations between Washington and Caracas, including an arrangement granting the United States access to Venezuelan oilfields.
This move is seen as a significant development in the evolving relationship between the two nations, with Rodriguez expected to play a role in proposed changes to Venezuela's oil legislation.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / AFP / Reuters / Al Jazeera

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in international drug trafficking and terrorism financing networks, aiming to disrupt their operations and financial flows.

These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued commitment to combating illicit activities that pose threats to national security and global stability. The designations aim to isolate these networks from the international financial system.

The specific details of the designated individuals and entities, along with the reasons for their inclusion, are outlined in the official OFAC announcement, providing clarity for financial institutions and other stakeholders regarding compliance obligations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 09, 2026. This license provides specific authorizations for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to clarify the scope of sanctions, facilitate humanitarian aid, or allow for certain routine commercial activities that do not undermine the core objectives of the sanctions regime.
This new General License reflects OFAC's ongoing efforts to manage the complexities of the Russia sanctions program, providing necessary flexibility while maintaining pressure on the Russian economy.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Issues Iran-related General License and Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 08, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities that support the Iranian regime's destabilizing actions. Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License to permit certain transactions.

In addition to the Iran-focused actions, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License. This amendment aims to refine existing authorizations or prohibitions within the Russia sanctions program, responding to evolving geopolitical and economic considerations.

These coordinated actions demonstrate OFAC's continued focus on both Iran and Russia, utilizing a combination of targeted sanctions and general licenses to achieve its foreign policy and national security objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals, Updates, and Publishes Iran-related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 05, 2026. These actions reflect ongoing reviews of sanctions lists and adjustments based on new information or changes in circumstances.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert and an Amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The alert provides important guidance regarding potential sanctions risks associated with Iran, while the amended FAQ offers clarification on specific aspects of the Iran sanctions program.

These publications are crucial for businesses and individuals to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions, particularly given the complexities of the Iran sanctions regime and the potential for severe penalties for violations.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil penalty of $11,662,930.

The settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. This action is part of a broader enforcement effort by the Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.
Bank of America admitted to willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and failures in its anti-money laundering program, which contributed to the sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) reached a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, resulting in a civil penalty of $175,015. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The details of the violations are outlined in the settlement agreement, which is publicly available. This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs across various industries.
Companies involved in international logistics and shipping are particularly susceptible to sanctions risks and are expected to implement robust compliance programs to prevent violations.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $1,427,230 against an individual for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This enforcement action underscores OFAC's authority to pursue penalties against individuals as well as corporate entities.

The specific nature of the violations committed by the individual is detailed in the public enforcement information. OFAC's actions serve as a reminder that individuals involved in transactions subject to U.S. jurisdiction must also adhere to sanctions compliance requirements.
This penalty reinforces the importance of due diligence and understanding sanctions obligations for all parties engaged in international financial and commercial activities.

This settlement highlights the need for companies across various sectors to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs.

The enforcement action against Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. demonstrates OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions, even for smaller-scale violations. The details of the case are available in the public settlement agreement.

This penalty serves as a reminder to all businesses, regardless of their size or industry, that they must diligently screen their transactions and business partners against OFAC's sanctions lists to avoid potential violations.

articles.headline: Pakistan Suspends Iran Border Trade Amid Security Concerns and Violence
body: Pakistan has halted trade with Iran at the Taftan and Gabd-Rimdan crossings in Balochistan province, leaving approximately 2,000 trucks stranded on both sides of the border. The suspension, which emerged on Saturday, has been attributed to security concerns by Pakistani officials, while Iran points to technical issues.
This border closure comes amidst ongoing violence and heightened tensions between the two nations, with Pakistan citing the need to improve border management for counterterrorism efforts.

Despite the trade suspension, passenger traffic at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has reportedly continued. The move highlights the delicate regional dynamics and the impact of security concerns on cross-border economic activities.

articles.headline: Trump Pauses New Russia Sanctions, Citing Need to Analyze Global Economic Impact
body: U.S. President Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. The legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, had sought to clamp down on financial resources fueling Russia's war against Ukraine.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the 60-day pause is intended to allow for an analysis of the sanctions' impact on the global economy and the U.S. economy, noting that various conflicts are affecting global energy prices.

The move, which includes waiving many sanctions, restrictions, and duties on Russia, has been met with approval by Russian officials and comes amid Trump's public criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a record-setting $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread breakdowns in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

This penalty, the largest in OCC history, comes nearly two years after the bank entered into a cease-and-desist order to address its long-standing BSA deficiencies. Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould stated that the bank's 'poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable.'

The OCC found that Bank of America's deficient transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, posing significant risks to U.S. national and economic security. This action underscores the OCC's commitment to swift and significant action against banks with ineffective BSA/AML programs.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express on October 08, 2026. This action was taken due to significant deficiencies in the company's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.
This enforcement action, alongside parallel consent orders from the Federal Reserve, highlights the OCC's focus on ensuring robust financial crimes compliance across the banking sector.

The OCC's findings underscore the importance for financial institutions to not only meet regulatory requirements but also to ensure their risk assessments accurately reflect their business operations and that senior management effectively oversees remediation efforts for any identified deficiencies.

articles.headline: BIS Expands Export Controls on Semiconductor Manufacturing Items and Modifies Entity List
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published a rule on October 13, 2022, implementing expanded controls on certain advanced computing integrated circuits and semiconductor manufacturing equipment when exported, reexported, or transferred (in-country) to the People's Republic of China or Macau.

This rule implements additional controls on semiconductor equipment, as well as related technology and software, and clarifies existing semiconductor equipment parameters and the control structure under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

These actions are taken to further the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States, reflecting a continued focus on restricting China's access to advanced semiconductor technology.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
